transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess… what brings me in is I just can’t shake this heavy feeling. It’s like fear and guilt all mixed together, and I’m tense pretty much all day, waiting for something else to go wrong. I keep blaming myself for not stopping what happened.

Sorry, I know that probably sounds vague. I work around construction sites, so I’m used to checking things and looking for what could go wrong, and now it’s like my brain won’t stop doing that even when I’m not at work.
Can you tell me more about what happened that you feel guilty about and how it’s been affecting you?

I feel guilty because I keep thinking I should’ve stopped it, like I should’ve seen it coming somehow. I know that sounds… I don’t know, maybe not totally fair to myself, but I keep replaying that part in my head.

And it’s been affecting me in this constant way. Like I’m just carrying this heavy feeling around—fear and guilt together—and I stay tense all day, like I’m waiting for the next thing to go wrong. Even when I’m doing normal stuff, I’m scanning for problems. I do that at work anyway, being around construction sites and inspections, but now it doesn’t shut off.
Can you tell me about the specific event or situation that you feel guilty about and keep replaying in your mind?

It was my husband falling. That’s the part I keep seeing.

I’ll be doing something totally normal at work, like measuring a railing, or I’ll hear a ladder scrape somewhere, and suddenly it’s like I can see him falling right in front of me. Not like I’m thinking about it on purpose—more like it just jumps into my head. My stomach drops and my hands get shaky.

And then I’ll be standing there with a tape measure in my hand, trying to act normal, but I’m not really there for a second. It’s embarrassing, honestly. I mean, I know ladders and railings are just part of the job, I’ve been around that stuff for years, but now those sounds or movements just… take me right back to it.
Since your husband’s fall, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities that remind you of what happened?

Yeah… I have, though I didn’t really think of it that way at first. I’ve started turning down certain jobs if they involve raised porches or second-story decks. I tell myself it’s scheduling or that somebody else is better for it, and sometimes that’s kind of true, but… not really.

And at home, I find reasons not to talk about the repair. Like I’ll suddenly need to do laundry or check an email or something stupid. I also avoid looking at the spot where it happened. Which is hard, because it’s just part of the house, you know? But I’ll walk around it like if I don’t look directly at it, I can keep it from starting up in my head.
Since your husband’s fall, have you noticed yourself being especially alert or easily startled by things that remind you of the accident, even if they’re not directly dangerous?

I don’t know… I mean, maybe a little? I’m not sure I’d call it “easily startled.” I do notice certain noises more now, like if something clanks or someone drops a tool, but on job sites that happens all the time anyway, so it’s hard to tell what’s normal and what’s me making it into something.

Sometimes I think I’m just paying closer attention because that’s what I do for work, you know? Like last week I spent way too long arguing with myself about whether a handrail was actually loose or if I was just being picky, and then I got distracted thinking about how our old neighbor used to complain about every little code thing when we were renovating—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… I guess I’ve noticed I’m more aware of stuff like that, but I don’t really know if I’m more startled exactly.
Have you noticed that your emotional state has stayed mostly negative since your husband’s fall—like ongoing fear, guilt, or shame that doesn’t seem to go away?

Yeah… that’s probably the main reason I’m here, honestly.

It’s like this heavy feeling I can’t put down. Fear, I guess, and guilt mixed together. I’ll be doing normal things and part of me is just tense, like I’m waiting for the next thing to go wrong. And then I start going over what I should’ve noticed, what I should’ve done differently.

I know people say accidents happen, and I’ve said that to clients a million times, actually—like when a stair tread isn’t to code or someone used the wrong fastener and they’re trying to explain it away—but when it’s your own house, your own husband, it doesn’t feel that simple. It feels like I should have stopped it somehow.

So yeah. It hasn’t really gone away. It’s just kind of there most of the time.
